main_sections.title: The World of Limitless Possibilities
main_sections.prose_summary: This informational text introduces the Paralympic Games as a global platform that celebrates resilience and extraordinary talent of athletes with locomotor, sensory, or intellectual disabilities. Bharat's Paralympic journey dates to 1968, with the first medal won in swimming in 1972. The text centres on a detailed interview with Dr. Deepa Malik — Khel Ratna, Arjuna, and Padma Shri awardee — one of the 10 most inspirational women para-athletes globally as recognised by the International Paralympic Committee. At 29, Dr. Malik was diagnosed with a spinal tumour; post-surgery she was declared permanently paralysed waist down and wheelchair-bound. Faced with two choices — squandering her life in remorse or transforming it into a world of limitless possibilities — she chose the latter. Drawing on her pre-existing love of swimming, she transitioned to para-athletics. Her breakthrough came at the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games where she won silver in the shot-put event. She holds multiple 'firsts': first Indian female para-athlete to win an Asian Games medal in athletics, and India's first female Paralympic medallist across any sport. She articulates that physical limitations do not define potential and champions the philosophy of 'ability beyond disability'. Challenges she overcame included societal underestimation, which she met with mental resilience, family support, and fortitude. She views Paralympics as a force that breaks preconceived notions about disability. Beyond sport, Dr. Malik advocates for disability rights: she strengthens the emotional health of persons with challenges, empowers women through outdoor sports, provides equipment to para sportspersons, and organises disability-sports awareness sessions in schools and colleges. Her closing advice — every setback is an opportunity to prove strength; disability is not a limitation but a unique strength waiting to be unleashed — encapsulates the chapter's central theme.

main_sections.title: Nine Gold Medals
main_sections.poem_text:
1. The athletes had come from all over the country
To run for the gold, for the silver, and bronze
Many weeks and months of training
All coming down to these games.

2. The spectators gathered around the old field
To cheer on all the young women and men
The final event of the day was approaching
Excitement was high to begin.

3. The blocks were all lined up for those who would use them
The hundred-yard dash and the race to be run
These were nine resolved athletes in the back of the starting line
Poised for the sound of the gun.

4. The signal was given, the pistol exploded
And so did the runners all charging ahead
But the smallest among them, he stumbled and staggered
And fell to the asphalt instead.

5. He gave out a cry of frustration and anguish
His dreams and his efforts dashed in the dirt
But as sure as I'm standing here telling this story
The same goes for what next occurred.

6. The eight other runners pulled up on their heels
The ones who had trained for so long to compete
One by one they all turned round and went back to help him
And brought the young boy to his feet.

7. Then all the nine runners joined hands and continued
The hundred-yard dash now reduced to a walk
And a banner above that said (Special Olympics)
Could not have been more on the mark.

8. That's how the race ended, with nine gold medals
They came to the finish line holding hands still
And a standing ovation and nine beaming faces
Said more than these words ever will.

— David Roth
main_sections.poem_appreciation_summary: Written by David Roth, 'Nine Gold Medals' celebrates the spirit of the Special Olympics through an eight-stanza narrative poem. Set at the final event of a track meet, nine athletes prepare for the hundred-yard dash. When the smallest competitor stumbles and falls, the other eight stop, turn back, and help him to his feet; together they walk the race to the finish line, holding hands, to receive nine gold medals and a standing ovation. The dominant theme is empathy and collective humanity over individual competition. The tone shifts from anticipatory excitement in the early stanzas to grief and anguish at the fall, before settling into warm affirmation at the close. Key imagery includes the pistol's explosion, the asphalt fall, and the joined hands crossing the finish line. Alliteration ('stumbled and staggered'), auditory imagery ('cry of frustration and anguish', 'pistol exploded'), and visual imagery ('nine beaming faces', 'standing ovation') give the poem its emotional texture. The final line — 'Said more than these words ever will' — underscores that the athletes' act of solidarity transcends language.

listening.transcript_text: Good morning, dear listeners! If you're feeling a bit low today, I've something to share that will inspire you to push your boundaries. I'm going to talk about an inspirational personality, Patrick Gomes, a special athlete and coach. He is a talented special athlete whose journey began with his participation in various track events way back in 1991, in Chennai. However, it was only in 1995, as a student at Okhla Centre of Learning and Development, that he was selected in football for the Special Olympics World Summer Games held at Connecticut, in the USA. That became a milestone in his life, changing his life forever. He participated in several special games after that, primarily football. Later, he represented Special Olympics Bharat in Spain for a World Athletics Championship. Gradually, he trained as a coach. He has been coaching special athletes for over 15 years now in sports and related values. He strongly believes that sports is important for everyone as it brings positivity, fitness, and discipline. He jogs for two hours every day. Despite his speech challenge, he is quite an independent and confident person; he lives all by himself, doing all the daily chores at home.
